# Chapter One: The Bell at Low Tide

## Scene: The Lower Pier

At low tide, Greywater Harbor showed its bones. Black pilings leaned out of the mud, old chains lay in rusted loops, and the narrow channel to the sea looked more like a road than water. Mara Venn crossed the lower pier with a lantern in one hand and her grandfather's brass key in the other.

The bell had rung at dawn, though the bell tower had been empty for thirty-two years. Everyone in Greywater knew that because everyone had a version of the story. Some said the old keeper drowned. Some said he walked into the sea on purpose. Mara only knew that the rope had been cut before she was born, yet three clear notes had rolled across the roofs that morning.

'You heard it too,' said Tomas Reed from behind a stack of lobster pots. He was trying to sound casual and failing. His coat was buttoned wrong, and a smear of ink crossed one cheek. 'Before you ask, no, I did not ring anything.'

Mara held up the brass key. 'My grandfather left this in the sugar jar with a note that said: Lower door. Do not open after the third bell.'

Tomas stared at the key. 'And naturally your plan is to open the lower door.'

'We've only had one bell.'

'That is not the reassuring mathematics you think it is.'

They reached the end of the pier, where a stone stair descended into green shadow. At the bottom waited a narrow iron door set into the seawall. Salt had furred its hinges white. Above the keyhole someone had scratched three words into the stone: LISTEN BEFORE ENTERING.

Mara pressed her ear to the metal. At first she heard only the sucking retreat of the tide. Then came a faint mechanical ticking, slow and patient, from somewhere beyond the door.

Tomas whispered, 'Please tell me clocks are normal under the harbor.'

Mara slid the key into the lock. It turned with almost no resistance.

***

## Scene: The Locked Boathouse

The passage beyond the seawall smelled of wet rope, lamp oil, and cold stone. Their lantern light found a row of hooks, a broken oar, and a painted board listing tides from a year long before either of them was born.

Halfway down the corridor stood a desk sealed beneath a sheet of cloudy glass. A logbook rested on top. The final entry was dated the night the keeper vanished.

Tomas read aloud. 'Bell mechanism checked. North lens shuttered. Visitor arrived at eleven forty. Visitor refused to give a name.' He turned the page and frowned. 'The next line is strange.'

In the old logbook, someone had written [[Mina]] in double brackets beside a blot of dried blue ink. The marks meant nothing to Mara, but they were distinctive enough that she copied them into her pocket notebook exactly as written.

Below the name was a second sentence: If the lantern burns blue, do not answer the bell.

A sound rolled through the passage.

BONG.

The iron door slammed shut behind them.

Tomas went pale. 'Two bells.'

Mara's lantern flame narrowed, shivered, and turned blue.

# Chapter Two: The Lantern Room

## Scene: The Keeper's Stair

The hidden stair climbed inside the seawall and emerged in the abandoned lantern room above the harbor. Greywater spread beneath them in silver roofs and chimney smoke, while the sea beyond the breakwater had begun to return with the tide.

The room should have been empty. Instead, every brass surface gleamed as though polished that morning. A kettle sat warm on a little stove. On the circular table lay three cups, two clean and one stained dark at the rim.

Tomas touched the kettle and snatched his hand back. 'Someone is here.'

Mara looked toward the great lamp. Its glass lens was dark, but a thin blue radiance pulsed behind the metal shutters. Each pulse matched the ticking they had heard below.

On the wall hung a harbor map marked with seven red circles. Six surrounded wrecks that Mara knew from local stories. The seventh circle sat over open water north of the lighthouse, where no wreck had ever been recorded.

A folded scrap of paper had been pinned there with a fishhook. It read: WHEN THE THIRD BELL RINGS, THE CHANNEL OPENS.

Mara heard footsteps on the spiral stair below. Slow. Measured. One step at a time.

Tomas lifted the nearest object he could find, which happened to be a brass umbrella stand. 'I would like it noted that this is a terrible weapon.'

'Noted,' Mara whispered.

The footsteps stopped just beneath the trapdoor.

***

## Scene: The Last Ring

The trapdoor rose an inch, then settled. No hand appeared. Instead, a man's voice came through the gap, calm and tired.

'If the lamp is blue, don't let it see the sea.'

Mara and Tomas exchanged a look. She crossed the room and pulled the first shutter closed. Tomas understood and took the next. Together they circled the lamp, sealing one panel after another until only the north-facing shutter remained.

The blue light brightened. Beyond the glass, the returning tide filled the harbor channel in a glittering rush.

BONG.

The third bell shook dust from the rafters.

Mara slammed the final shutter closed. For one heartbeat, something enormous moved beneath the water north of the breakwater, outlined by blue light. Then darkness swallowed it.

The trapdoor opened. An elderly man in a keeper's coat climbed into the room, breathing hard. His left sleeve was soaked to the elbow.

Tomas pointed the umbrella stand at him. 'Name.'

The man looked at the absurd weapon, then at Mara's brass key. 'Elias Venn,' he said. 'And if you're holding that key, then my brother finally decided thirty-two years was long enough to keep a secret.'

Mara forgot the bell, the blue light, and the impossible shape beneath the water. 'My grandfather said you drowned.'

Elias gave a weary smile. 'Greywater has always preferred a simple story.'

Outside, the tide climbed the harbor wall, and somewhere beneath the sealed lamp, the mechanism began ticking again.
